profile.campus_mw_context: The 128,715-sq. ft. data center in Sterling, VA, offers 11 MW of IT capacity and features robust connectivity options with high bandwidth and high-availability circuits and a number of metro and long-haul networks.

reading.body:
CyrusOne NVA4 in Sterling offers 11 MW of IT capacity across 128,715 square feet, which translates to roughly 275 racks at typical AI training density of 40 kW per rack.

The facility emphasizes network connectivity with multiple metro and long-haul circuits available. For distributed training workloads that move large volumes of data between nodes, network quality becomes a binding constraint. Sterling's proximity to Washington Dulles and major fiber routes positions it to serve that need rather than to concentrate raw compute power in one location.

Virginia has 330 mapped data centers but only 25 publish capacity figures. NVA4 ranks 26th among those with disclosed capacity at 11 MW, representing less than 1% of Virginia's 1,603 MW of published capacity. The state's true infrastructure footprint is largely hidden, with 305 facilities either unmapped or not reporting power figures. This opacity means aggregate Virginia capacity for frontier AI work cannot yet be assessed from public data.

The facility's modest scale and lack of published power infrastructure details beyond IT load suggest it is unlikely to host large-scale training runs or frontier model development. It is positioned for enterprise workloads, specialized compute, or distributed inference where network quality matters more than absolute power density. Whether modest regional data centers matter to AI scaling depends on whether they collectively comprise meaningful capacity or serve as supporting infrastructure for larger campuses elsewhere.
